analysis.one_liner: Sets a national plan to cut U.S. oil use by 8 million barrels a day by 2030.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2010 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the President to build a national plan to cut U.S. oil consumption by 8 million barrels per day by 2030, set stricter fuel-economy and emissions standards for cars, trucks, and even planes and trains through 2030, and spend heavily to put electric vehicles on the road — including grants of up to $250 million each to selected "deployment communities" and bigger tax credits for electric car buyers there [S2]. It also extended and expanded tax credits for biofuel and natural gas vehicle industries and required utilities to plan for electric car charging [S2]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers would benefit from tighter fuel-economy standards that cut gasoline use, and residents of selected deployment communities would get larger, refundable electric-car tax credits ($5,000 instead of $2,500) plus publicly funded charging infrastructure [S2]. Electric vehicle makers, battery makers, charging-infrastructure companies, electric utilities, biofuel producers, and natural gas vehicle manufacturers would gain from a long list of tax credits, grants, bond financing, and loan guarantees [S2]. Homeowners using heating oil, propane, or kerosene would get federal funding for efficiency upgrades and conversion to wood-pellet boilers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, EV buyers, and clean-energy industries

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a binding national goal of reducing U.S. oil consumption by 8 million barrels per day by 2030 and requires the President to produce a plan to meet it [S2].

It directs the Transportation Department and EPA to write joint fuel-economy and greenhouse-gas standards for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles for model years 2017–2030, plus standards for planes, trains, boats, and construction equipment [S2].

It authorizes $2 billion for a program to deploy 700,000 plug-in electric vehicles in up to 15 competitively selected communities, with grants of up to $250 million per community for charging infrastructure and purchase incentives [S2].

Buyers of new plug-in electric vehicles in deployment communities would get an increased, refundable tax credit they could transfer to the dealer at purchase, and the per-manufacturer cap on the credit would rise from 200,000 to 300,000 vehicles [S3].

It extends biodiesel, renewable diesel, cellulosic biofuel, and alcohol fuel tax credits, adds an investment tax credit for advanced biofuel facilities, and allows tax credits for natural gas vehicles [S2].
It raises the tax-excluded commuter benefit to $230 per month and funds freight-rail projects aimed at moving 10% of truck freight to rail or water by 2020 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost of the new grant programs, battery prize fund, and expanded tax credits for electric vehicles, biofuel plants, and natural gas vehicles, several of which are permanent extensions of existing industry credits [S2]. Oil producers and refiners would lose demand as fuel-economy standards tighten and electric vehicles proliferate [S2]. Car buyers could face higher sticker prices as manufacturers meet stricter fuel-economy requirements [S3]. The bill also directs every electric utility to develop plans to support plug-in vehicles and allows regulators to consider letting utilities recover those costs from ratepayers [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes more than $2 billion for the deployment communities program alone, plus a 500-mile Battery Fund and new refundable tax credits, all of which add to federal deficits [S2].
Several biofuel and alcohol fuel tax credits would be extended or expanded, continuing taxpayer support for established fuels that already receive subsidies [S2].
Tighter fuel-economy and emissions standards for 2017–2030 model years would push up vehicle manufacturing costs, a cost that typically shows up in purchase prices [S3].

The bill creates a new National Energy Security Council in the White House and directs every electric utility to file plans for electric vehicles, with regulators able to approve cost recovery — meaning some of the compliance cost could land on electricity bills [S2].
The bill's oil-savings goal can be adjusted by the President, so the headline 8-million-barrel target was not guaranteed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers, the promise was lower fuel costs, more charging infrastructure, and less exposure to volatile world oil prices, which the bill itself notes cost the U.S. a $380 billion petroleum trade deficit in 2008 [S3]. The tradeoff is real: the money comes from federal borrowing and expanded tax expenditures, some of it for established industries like biofuel and natural gas rather than for consumers directly, and utility compliance costs could reach ratepayers. A supporter would call it a down payment on energy independence; a skeptic would call it a bundle of industry subsidies wrapped around a fuel-economy standard.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-July 2010, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on July 15, 2010, with three Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over the tax provisions central to the bill, took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote appear in its action history [S5].
With no floor action, the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil industry and the transportation status quo were better off: the stricter fuel-economy standards, electric-vehicle deployment grants, and utility planning requirements never took effect, and the projected reduction in oil demand never happened. Clean-energy industries that would have received the credits and grants gained nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers and the fuel status quo

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled three Senate Democratic cosponsors

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Max Baucus)
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 15, 2010 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Senate Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so partisan support or opposition was never tested on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Stricter fuel-economy standards, a mandated 8-million-barrel-per-day reduction in oil consumption, and electric-vehicle deployment would cut directly into oil demand. Consumers would benefit from lower fuel use, which is precisely what the industry loses [S2].

Tighter 2017–2030 fuel-economy and emissions standards would raise compliance costs, but raised electric-vehicle credits, a higher 300,000-vehicle per-manufacturer cap, and deployment grants create a subsidized market for plug-in vehicles [S2][S3].

Every utility would have to plan for electric-vehicle charging, tax-exempt bonds and loan guarantees would fund charging infrastructure, and regulators could approve recovering the costs from ratepayers — locking in EV load as a new, publicly supported revenue stream [S2][S3].

The bill extends cellulosic, biodiesel, renewable diesel, and alcohol fuel credits and adds an investment tax credit for advanced biofuel facilities, including algae-based fuel. This continues taxpayer support for an industry whose product competes with oil [S2].

industries.industry: Natural gas vehicle and fuel industry
industries.note: New tax credits for natural gas vehicles, tax-exempt natural gas vehicle bonds, and an expensing deduction for manufacturing facilities subsidize natural gas as a transportation fuel, modestly reducing oil dependence [S2].
A $10 million battery prize, R&D funding, loan guarantees for charging networks, and the deployment-community grants channel federal money toward battery and charging equipment suppliers [S2].
